utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can the interpreters hear me? I'm glad to see that they're there. Good morning to the counsel for the Prosecution, to counsel for the Defence; good morning, General Krstic. For the record, we're still hearing the case against General Krstic, and we will continue with the testimony that we started yesterday. So without much further ado, I will give the floor to Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. We are coming towards the end of Mr. Mandzic's testimony. So with your permission, if the witness could be brought back into the courtroom, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mandzic. Did you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is the translation all right today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let me just remind you, Mr. Mandzic, that you are still testifying under an oath. You will continue answering questions that Mr. Cayley is going to put to you, and thank you for coming back this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandzic.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We left off with your testimony last night on the night of the 11th of July, 1995, when you returned from Bratunac to the UN Compound in Potocari, and I'd now like to move ahead in time to the 12th of July of 1995, in the morning. You're inside the UN Compound. Can you describe to the Judges the scene that you saw in and around the compound at Potocari and inside the compound on the morning of the 12th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. At the base of the Dutch Battalion in Potocari, approximately 5.000 refugees had found temporary shelter. Most of them were elderly people, weak people. There were dozens of wounded as well. Most of them had been wounded in the shelling, shelling that was perpetrated by the VRS against the surrounding villages. The accommodation was by no means adequate. People were lying on the floor of old factory halls and also around the Dutch Battalion base, in the street and the surrounding factories. Altogether there were around 25.000 refugees who had gathered there. They had the same problems as those in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How hot was it that day, Mr. Mandzic?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The temperature was above 30 degrees Celsius. It was exhausting due to the temperature as well, let alone the fear. There was a shortage of water, of food. There were no toilet facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The children and the babies, what was their state at this time?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, the children were in a very difficult situation. As I have already stated, there was no food, so their mothers couldn't feed them. Their mothers were exhausted as well. So were the children. They were crying all the time, screaming. They had nothing to change them or to wash them. It was very sad to watch all this. When I try to think about it all, when I try to go back and reflect on it, I really see that it was a terrible trauma for all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At 10.00 that morning, Colonel Karremans called you again. Can you tell the Judges why he called you and what you did after your conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me go back to the previous night, that is, the night between the 11th and the 12th of July, and the first meeting in Bratunac with the representatives of the military authorities of Republika Srpska. General Mladic made an ultimatum. He demanded from the Dutch Battalion and from us that we should be back to Bratunac on the following day at 10.00 together with a Bosniak delegation that would be representing the refugees. So according to that, we organised ourselves. On the 12th of July, at 10.00 a.m., we were again in Bratunac together with the representatives of the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Whereabouts in Bratunac did you go on that morning?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was held at the same place, in the Fontana Hotel in Bratunac, like the first meeting, the one that had taken place on the night before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You referred to a Bosniak delegation. Apart from yourself, who were the members of that delegation?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Bosniak delegation were, well, myself, and then Mr. Ibro Nuhanovic, who did not survive the Srebrenica Calvary. In the afternoon, on the 13th of July, he was separated from his family by the forces of the VRS, and I haven't heard of him since that day. The third member of the Bosniak delegation was Mrs. Camila Omanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you can recall, who were the Dutch officers who accompanied you to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. It was the Commander of the Dutch Battalion. At that time he was a Lieutenant Colonel, Colonel Karremans. Then there was a Major from the Dutch Battalion, Major Boering. As far as I can remember, the third officer of the Dutch Battalion, who was a Sergeant, whom I remember very well but I just cannot remember his name at the moment, but I am able to recognise him, and I recognised him yesterday on the photograph that you showed me. Now, I have shown you video extracts of that meeting, which I'm not going to show in the courtroom for your evidence, but if you could briefly tell the Judges what you recall of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the second meeting, the one that started on the 12th of July at 10.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Mandzic.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meeting resembled more or less the previous one, the one that had taken place the night before, with one exception. During that meeting, while we were discussing, somebody approached the group, the meeting, from the side and addressed General Mladin, saying that the Bosniaks were arriving in the football stadium in Bratunac. So when we heard that, we were very upset. But then I glanced at my watch and I realised that within half an hour it was physically impossible for thousands of refugees to reach Bratunac from Potocari. Therefore it was a kind of provocation, whose objective was to scare the representatives of the Bosniak delegation, to disarm them, if one can put it that way, when it comes to their requests and their demands. They simply wanted to crush us, both physically and morally, so that we would be completely useless. Let me mention one other fact which can support this. One member of our negotiating group, our negotiating team, sustained a very severe psychological shock that day, a nervous breakdown.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall anything else that was discussed at that meeting, Mr. Mandzic?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was certain indications also about the possible evacuation of the population, but nothing really tangible, nothing specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall who was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the officers from the command of the VRS, two civilian representatives of the Bratunac municipality attended the meeting, as far as I can remember. One of them was Miroslav Deronjic, who at the time was the president of the Serb Democratic Party for the Bratunac municipality. The other one was Milisav, I believe his name is, Milisav Simic, who was the president of the Bratunac Municipal Assembly at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you name, if you can, the individuals from the VRS Command that were present at that meeting on the morning of the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. I remember very well that next to General Mladic sat General Krstic, who is here today, together with some other officers, whose faces I can remember very well, but I'm not quite sure as to their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall whether Mr. Miroslav Deronjic said anything at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall, but I do remember, on the other hand, that Simic said something.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what Simic said at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Simic spoke to General Mladic at one point and he told him that in respect of certain Bosniaks, they needed to have some informative talks. He suspected that they had been members of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall what time that meeting finished?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It finished between -- sometime between 11.00 and 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: After the meeting, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the meeting we went back, together with the officers of the Dutch Battalion. We went back to their camp. The situation was very difficult. We were trying to figure out what to do next, because it was obvious that no firm guarantees had been given that there would be a positive solution for all those refugees. Mr. Ibro Nuhanovic, Mrs. Omanovic, Camila, and myself, we were very concerned and we were thinking of putting down the names of the refugees on paper, but at that time it was a very difficult thing to do. Do you want me to say perhaps that during the first meeting, General Mladic had promised that everybody, regardless of their age, sex, and so on, would, according to their wishes, be evacuated. Later on we would see that it was by no means an evacuation, but a very cruel deportation. Mladic repeated several times those words, that he would allow for an evacuation to happen for all those people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You mentioned General Mladic. Did he appear that day in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did appear in Potocari on that day, between 12.00 and 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At that time, at 12.00 or 1.00, had the deportation started by that time, the movement of the population to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember it correctly, General Mladic came to Potocari. He simply entered this mass of refugees sometime between noon and 1.00 p.m. And I think that the deportation began after 1.00 on that day, on the 12th of July, that is, after General Mladic had left Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So can you give an approximate time when the movement of the population started?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 1.00 p.m. on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Judges what you saw taking place in respect of that movement?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, 1995, in the afternoon hours, I was in the Dutch Battalion camp. I was in a position to observe, like everybody else who had remained in the camp, that women, children were boarding buses. We could see dozens of buses waiting in line, waiting for the population to board them. So because of that, we concluded that there was a separation of the population going on at the time. We could only see women and children on those buses. We didn't know where the men were between 15/16 and 60 years of age. This additionally upset us, but we were completely helpless. We couldn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move ahead to the early evening hours of the 12th of July. I think the Dutch Commander, Colonel Karremans, came to speak to you. Can you tell the Judges what happened after he spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the afternoon hours on that day between 5.00 and 6.00 p.m., to be precise, Major Franken from the Dutch Battalion spoke to me and Mr. Nuhanovic. He told us that we had to get out of the Dutch Battalion camp in Potocari because some officers of the VRS were expecting us outside the camp. So this is how me and late Mr. Nuhanovic went towards the gate of the camp. While we were moving towards the gate, which was open at that time, a Serb soldier of a heavy build started running towards us, and he went straight for Mr. Ibro Nuhanovic. He expressed his anger and his hatred by addressing Mr. Nuhanovic with a question, "Are you a Turk?" Nuhanovic remained silent. However, this didn't stop the Serb soldier, who landed a heavy blow on Mr. Nuhanovic, who, as a result of that blow, fell down. Standing next to us there was a Dutch officer, a Sergeant, who saw this happening, and at that moment he reacted by saying, "No. No. It's not correct." Then the Serb soldiers moved away. We continued for another 10 or 15 metres, and then General Mladic got out of a car, and he ordered us to come with him towards the centre of this mass of people who had gathered in Potocari. General Mladic ordered me and Mr. Nuhanovic to speak to the people, though we actually had nothing to tell them because our fate was the same as those 30.000 people. But I do remember that General Mladic addressed the refugees, and he told them once again, "Do not panic. You will all be safe. You will all be evacuated to the area," or, rather, "the areas that are under the control of the BH army. First the old and the infirm, then mothers with their children, and then everybody will follow as well." But what created additional panic on that day was the fact that as early as in the morning of that day, that is, before 12.00, the soldiers of the VRS, who on the previous night had surrounded the Dutch Battalion camp and the civilian population, those soldiers, in the early morning hours on that day, had pierced the corridor and actually mingled with the population. So on that day, a search for certain Bosniaks started, with no apparent reason at all. They also started taking them out from the group, and we do not know anything about those individuals. We could see nearby houses on fire. They also torched the houses in a selective manner, with the purpose of frightening the population and also so as to prevent them from coming back. It was a very clear message, very clear sign that Srebrenica -- that is, that there would be no life for Bosniaks in Srebrenica anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: After Mladic had addressed the crowd and you had been outside the compound, did you return inside the UN Dutch compound?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and late Ibro Nuhanovic went back to the camp of the Dutch soldiers, and spent again the night in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you hear anything that night?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that is what still causes me problems. It is voices, incomprehensible voices and some blunt blows, such sounds. On that night, between the 12th and the 13th of July, I could not really establish where they came from since we were, as I said, in the compound of the Dutch Battalion in Potocari, and it was a building which was additionally reinforced with concrete slabs by the Dutch soldiers in order to improve their safety in case they were attacked, in case the Dutch soldiers were attacked. That night, I repeat, I heard but -- I heard some shots but not very clearly. I heard some screams, noise, but I could not really say which direction they all came from, these sounds came from, because the whole building was plated with those concrete slabs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit 5/2, and also if you have available 5/6.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, you stated to the Judges that you were inside the compound that night, in a building that had been reinforced against gunfire by concrete slabs. Could you indicate on this photograph where you stayed that night, on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th of July I was in the Dutch base or, rather, the building that was -- that the officers -- where the officers were quartered, and according to this photograph, it is here [indicated].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is pointing to the building which is in the uppermost left-hand corner of the yellow square, the square which delineates the UN base. If the witness could now be shown Exhibit 5/6.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, do you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes. This is an industrial plant, the 11 of March Factory, which was one of the Energoinvest units in this building, and in front of it by its fence posts is the road, Bratunac-Potocari-Srebrenica. On the 11th, 12th, 13th of July, there were tens of thousands of people forcibly amassed in that area. I can also say that in this building or, rather, in this hall, in this plant, that I was there on the 11th of July, and I was there until 9.00, until I was called to go to the Commander of the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandzic. We've finished with those exhibits. Let's move ahead in time, Mr. Mandzic, to the 13th of July, and if you can tell the Judges rumours you were beginning to hear on that morning in respect of the men, of the Bosniak men who were present in and around Potocari.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That morning, the 13th of July, 1995, several acquaintances of mine who are no longer alive, that is, people who did not survive the Srebrenica Calvary, approached me and said, "They killed some people last night." The soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska were taking away men to nearby houses and killed them there outside the camp in which there was some 25.000 expellees. Nobody could sleep because screams could be heard all night long. And the man went on with his story and his experience. He have said, "So-and-so," and then he would mention a place near Skelani at Dobrak, was trying to kill himself, to commit suicide all night to prevent the soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska laying hands on him, but they, nevertheless, prevented him from that and then took it out on him. I heard identical stories, shortly afterwards, from people who, that morning, managed to jump over the fence where the Dutch soldiers were. And I was really scared, like everybody else. After that I went to see the deputy commander of the Dutch Battalion and asked him to try to put a stop to this type of evacuation, which was not evacuation, properly speaking; it was a very cruel deportation. And I remember that Major Franken, who was replacing Commander Karremans, said then, "Impossible." And I also remember what he said in English. He said, "I'm doing my best."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Mandzic, if you wish. If you have more to say to the Judges, I don't want to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Then I asked Major Franken, "Well, what next? Where's the way out of this? Because they will separate all men. Will any of the men survive? Shall we have any proof that people ever lived in this area, that there were some people there?" And Major Franken said, "Yes, let's do something. Let's try to make a list, at least in the camp, if we cannot do it outside the camp." So I began to do that straight away. I entered those destroyed structures, those plants of the factory in the camp, and with some other men I started compiling the list mostly of the male population between the ages of 17, 18 to 70 onward. I must also say that I had some trouble as I was compiling that list, first of all because some of the people from my -- from the same place were afraid of seeing their names on that list. I remember some said, "Right. We trust you, we know you, but what if our name is on this list and the army of the Republika Srpska gets hold of it?" But we did manage to make a list of men in that camp between the ages of 18 and 80, and there were 239 men on that list, even though there were many more of them in that camp, but for reasons that I mentioned, because people were afraid to see their name on the list, that the army of the Republika Srpska would get hold of that list, and they refused to give us names. I turned that list over to Major Franken and I was also faced with a major dilemma: What if this list with 239 names, what if the army of the Republika Srpska lays its hand on this list of 239 names? But Major Franken said, "Well, don't worry. If nothing else, I will put that list in my trousers and won't let them search me." And that is how it was. That list exists to this day, but those men are no longer alive. And it is of no help to their families, because they are still grieving and still searching for all those missing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, the evacuation outside the UN compound, the movement of this population, what time did it finish on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late afternoon, as far as I can remember, sometime around 1900.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The buses and trucks that were moving these people, were you able to see those trucks at close quarters, the buses and trucks?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could. I was about 200 meters away from them. And because I moved around the camp, so sometimes I came as close as 50 meters and I could see inscriptions on those buses, so that it was -- the deportation had been planned, and I concluded it because I saw such a large number of buses and trucks which had arrived from outside, by and large from towns such as Bijeljina, Banja Luka, Bratunac, and so on. I know -- I remember, that is, the inscriptions on these buses: Sembreija Transport from Bijeljina. That was a transporting company, a bussing company from before the war. Drina Trans, another bussing company from Zvornik which is still in operation. A bussing company from Banja Luka, I believe, called Auto Transport, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you manage to observe the state of the civilian population that were on those buses?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I could see from a distance of some 50 to 100 meters those were mothers, wives, sisters, crying, screaming, tearing their hair off, because they had boarded the buses and could leave, yet their next of kin -- their children, their fathers, brothers, husbands, and so on -- were not with them, even though they, on the 11th and the 12th of July, not to mention all the days before that, had been together, and that was a separation which I think hurt very badly. And to this day, if you could see those women, if you could see how they live, under what conditions, and their sorrow, which persists to this day, you would understand it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that there were people that had been wounded that were inside the compound in Potocari. What happened to those people on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A group of wounded was evacuated that day. But another group of people, who I believe had sustained more severe injuries, who were awaiting operations, they could not be transported and they stayed behind in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: On that day you mentioned earlier in your testimony that there were a large number of VRS personnel in and around the compound. Do you recall if any VRS soldiers or officers came into the compound at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. As I said -- as I have said, and I shall repeat it, it was already in the early morning hours of the 12th of July. The army of Republika Srpska entered Potocari and amongst the civilian population, with a view to intimidating them, especially, and taking away the male population, so when the evacuation was on its way, there was no choice. Men as of the age of 12 to one side, women and children to the other. But on the 13th of July, I remember how a VRS officer came into the camp, Momir Nikolic. Before the war he was an educator in Bratunac. Momir Nikolic, as he said, was tasked with checking who were those wounded, what age groups they belonged to, and how had they sustained their wounds. I was not far from him when this officer, Momir Nikolic, asked a Bosniak who had been gravely wounded and was awaiting for the surgical operation in the camp, "Where were you wounded? And that Bosniak did not reply, yet Nikolic persisted, "You were wounded in combat, and as such, you may not be evacuated, transported for further treatment." He also approached some other wounded, and in the same way he asked them where they had been wounded, where had they spent the time of the war, and so on and so forth. And also that day in the camp I saw another officer of the army of Republika Srpska in glasses, aged less than 40, and I recognised him on a slide yesterday. I would recognise him, but I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit 43, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So it would be correct to say that Mr. Nikolic was actively involved in deciding which of the wounded could be moved from the UN compound and which of the wounded would remain in the UN compound?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, quite so. He was determining which group of the wounded would be transported for further medical treatment and which ones of the wounded would stay behind in Potocari. Yes, this is that officer of the army of Republika Srpska who came to the camp of Dutch soldiers on the 13th of July, and on the 11th and the 12th of July attended, was present at the meeting in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: For the purposes of the record, the witness is referring to a photograph of an individual wearing glasses in Exhibit 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you know, Mr. Mandzic, what was the position of Mr. Nikolic in the VRS? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people introduced him as a colonel, but I'm not sure that that was indeed so. As a colonel of a unit whose operational zone was Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that's all you know about Mr. Nikolic's position, is it?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Rather, they called him Colonel and that his zone of operations was the municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the movement of the population, do you recall what time the movement of the population that was still in the UN compound finished on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime around 1900 on the 13th of July, the Dutch soldiers' camp, where there were still some 5.000 people, but it was practically empty, the army of Republika Srpska ordered all the expellees, all the expelled, to come out of the camp so after 1900 there was only a small group of severely wounded, and a group of 27 Bosniaks who had been working for UNPROFOR or MSF as their local staff were left in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, since these were individuals that had been in the compound rather than outside the compound, were you able to observe more closely what was actually happening with these individuals that were being expelled?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what you saw taking place?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can, yes. On the 12th of July and on the 13th of July too, I saw and I watched women and small children board buses, trucks, and the scene which I described, women crying, children screaming, those women tearing their hair off, in pain because their next of kin had been separated from them. I could see that they were evacuating or, rather, deporting women and children. And in the same manner they evacuated or, rather, deported men from the Dutch Battalion compound, where there were some 5.000 people. One could invariably see one or two soldiers who would announce, "Now, this group. That group goes now. One hundred, 200, 300, move," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say that you saw men being deported, and by the manner of your evidence, are you saying that the men were being separated?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I watched from a distance of some 50 to 100 metres away how only women with small children boarded the buses, with children up -- from infants from up to 12, 13 years of age. I saw those women screaming, moaning, crying, tearing their hair off. On that day, the 13th of July, on the 12th of July, the same scene repeated over and over again. Everybody reacted in the same way. And I could see that male individuals, as of the age of 12 or 13, had been separated by force from their next of kin, from their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who was carrying out the separation of the men from their families?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, soldiers of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, speaking of these VRS soldiers, did you observe the uniforms and the insignia of these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. On the first day, on the 11th of July, and on the following day, on the 12th of July, as I was coming back from Bratunac on my way to Potocari, I could observe hundreds of soldiers standing next to the road, wearing uniforms, brand-new uniforms, I might say. Some of them were wearing the insignia of the VRS. Some didn't have any insignia at all. But they did have new military clothing. I could also hear various dialects, very just accents which did not resemble the dialect, the Ijekavski dialect, which is used by Bosnian Serbs in the region of Podrinje in Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's now move ahead in time. The compound is now empty. All of the refugees have gone. You're remaining with members of the Dutch Battalion. On the 17th of July, you signed a declaration with Major Franken.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness can now be shown Exhibit 47, which is the last new exhibit for this witness. There are four exhibits. There's 47A; 47B; 47C, which is the French translation; and 47D, which is the B/C/S translation. Mr. President, if I can explain in respect of this exhibit. There are, in fact, two English translations. The reason for that is that one of them, which I'll show on the ELMO, was a field translation that was done at the time, on the 17th of the July, in order to facilitate the signature of the representative of the Dutch Battalion. There are some inaccuracies in that translation. We have the original version there B/C/S, in the Bosnian language, and we have had that translated into English. So there is now an official English translation. But in order that the Court, as it were, sees all of the documents, there are, as I said, two English translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandzic, first of all --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Before I ask Mr. Mandzic any questions, can you put 47B on the ELMO? If you could move it up slightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandzic, is this the English version of this declaration that you signed on the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now -- if you could now put on the ELMO, I think it's 47D, which is the version in the witness's language. If you could turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This, Mr. Mandzic, is the version that you signed in your own language, and indeed Major Franken and a representative of the Bosnian Serb civilian authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be given the version in his own language. That's fine. The French and English translations, Your Honours, are the ones I would like you to follow, the French being 47C and the official English being 47A.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandzic, a few questions about this document. In the second paragraph, the document states that: "On 12 July 1995, in the Fontana Hotel in Bratunac, at our request negotiations were conducted between the representatives of our civilian authorities and the representatives of the Republika Srpska civilian authorities and the army regarding the evacuation of our civilian population from the Srebrenica enclave." Mr. Mandzic, is it accurate that that meeting was called at your request on the 12th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not accurate. You will remember that I said yesterday, and you could see it clearly on the video, that nobody from the Bosniak side ever requested negotiations, neither on the 11th, nor on the 12th of July. It was done upon the insistence of the VRS, and it was UNPROFOR who organised the first meeting in Bratunac on the 11th of July. Again, I must say these negotiations were not conducted at the request of the Bosniak side. We never requested these negotiations to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could move down through this document. We get to a section which says: "At the end of the negotiations between the two sides, the following was agreed," and the first paragraph states: "Our civilian population could stay in the enclave or move out, depending on the wish of each individual." Now, Mr. Mandzic, is this an accurate reflection of what actually happened on the 12th and 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not really. Not a single word from this paragraph reflects the events that were taking place on the 12th and the 13th of July and the following days as well. The International Committee for the Red Cross registered thousands of people who are still listed as missing. I would like to tell Your Honours, to state here before this Chamber, that the Bosniak representatives did not take part in the signing of this statement, and I assume neither did the representatives of the Dutch Battalion do so. This statement was a ready-made document which was prepared by the military and civilian authorities of the Republika Srpska, and it was presented to us as an ultimatum. It was presented also to the Dutch Battalion, as well as the Bosniak representatives, as an ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in the third paragraph following that paragraph it states: "It was arranged that the evacuation would be carried out by the army and police of Republika Srpska and that UNPROFOR would supervise and provide an escort for the evacuation." Is that statement an accurate reflection of what actually happened on the ground on the 12th and 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This paragraph is not an accurate reflection of the events and the facts that took place in Potocari and on the way from Potocari to Kladanj either. Kladanj is a small town in the area of Eastern Bosnia. It is actually the first town in the territory that was held by the soldiers of the BH army since 1995 -- 1992, I'm sorry, and this is where the Bosniak population was deported to in July 1995. As I said, this does not reflect the events, because the Dutch Battalion Major complained that on the night of the 11th and the 12th of July, had requisitioned almost every single vehicle and used them for deportation of the Bosniak population from Srebrenica. He could practically no longer send any soldier anywhere. They could not expose themselves to risk of an attack by the forces of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you're stating that in reality, there were very few convoys that were actually properly escorted by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only on the first day, on the 12th of July. On that day, the officers of the Dutch Battalion did send soldiers and vehicles to escort some of the buses carrying Bosniaks who were actually being deported by the VRS to the area of Kladanj. However, on the way from Potocari to Kladanj, according to Major Franken, his soldiers ran into obstacles that had been put up by soldiers of the VRS. They harassed them. They requisitioned their vehicles, vehicles belonging to the UNPROFOR forces. So they were unable to accomplish that mission. So on the following day, on the 13th of July, the deportation was carried out mostly without any escort or presence of the UNPROFOR forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the very last paragraph, and this may be something that you can't comment upon because you were not actually with any of the convoys, but the last paragraph states: "No incidents were provoked by any side during the evacuation, and the Serbian side observed all the regulations of the Geneva Conventions and the International Law of War." Then there is added, I think, a sentence by Major Franken: "As far as the convoys escorted by the UN forces were concerned." What do you say about that, Mr. Mandzic?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I already told Your Honours, the Serbian representatives, Deronjic, who represented the civilian government, appeared with this ready-made statement, and he made an ultimatum requesting that this statement be signed. However, he was very well aware of the situation. He knew that between the 13th and the 17th of July in Bratunac, a group of about several dozen wounded, whom I said had been evacuated on the 13th of July, had been retained. He also knew that there was still 27 Bosniaks in the camp, in addition to several other dozens of severely wounded persons. So that's what he had in mind. He said that we should sign the statement because human lives were at stake. So this was a kind of condition for all these persons that I have mentioned, all these categories of persons that I have mentioned, that they would be released. You must be aware of the situation, of the position in which some 450 soldiers of the Dutch Battalion had found themselves in. I've read this statement several times; that is, I read it several times at the time. I looked Major Franken in the eye, and he knew very well that this statement by no means reflected the real situation on the ground and the tragedy that ensued and that had happened actually. It was very ironical and cynical to invoke the Geneva Conventions, the provision regulating human rights and so on and so forth, especially the provisions of the International Law of War, for example. But as I must stress once again, on those days of July 1995, we were alone. We were helpless. The world was silent. They didn't know what was going on in Srebrenica or Potocari, or what to do in Srebrenica and Potocari. The International Community did not manage to send any representative of the International Red Cross, for example, UNHCR, United Nations to Srebrenica on that day. The only persons I know that had certain contacts were perhaps officers of the Dutch Battalion. He had perhaps contact with their command in the Netherlands, as well as other UNPROFOR commands in Bosnia. They were concerned about the fate of their soldiers. I, on the other hand, was concerned about the fate of my fellow citizens of Srebrenica. Of course, we didn't want any more blood to be shed, and we also wanted the soldiers of the Dutch Battalion to reach safely their homes. So we were all thinking in those lines. At that moment, Major Franken suggested, when he was presented with the statement by Deronjic, the representatives of the civilian authorities, that he adds this particular wording here: "As far as the convoys escorted by UN forces were concerned." This completely changed the meaning of this paragraph, and it actually meant that this statement could only refer to the evacuation as far as the persons escorted by the UN forces were concerned. According to what Dutch Battalion soldiers were saying on the 12th and the 13th of July, they managed to escort only two or three buses as far as Kladanj and that was that. There were hundreds of other buses, but in respect of those buses, they couldn't do anything, because their vehicles had already been requisitioned by VRS troops, together with all their equipment. So in view of the situation and in view of what Major Franken said, I simply signed this statement. Please, Your Honours, members of this Honourable Chamber, do consider this statement as an ultimatum that was put to us by members of the VRS in those days of the month of July 1995, when tens of thousands of people had been deported. And we didn't know what had happened to them. They had perhaps reached their destination, but at that time their destination was unknown to us. We were completely unable to inform ourselves about the situation through the media, for example. By signing this statement, we had in mind the fate of thousands of people, namely, the wounded persons who were still in the Dutch Battalion camp, about 27 Bosniaks who were still there, and we also had in mind the fate of the Dutch Battalion soldiers who were there in the area. It is very cynical that this statement should mention anything about the provisions of the Geneva Conventions and the International Law of War. However, it was our estimate at that time, and we were forced to sign it, because the fate of hundreds of people depended on our signature at that moment, despite the fact that we were actually not convinced that the fate of those hundreds of people and members of the Dutch battalion would have a positive outcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you wish, we could take a break now. I have about five minutes of my examination-in-chief remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think it's a very good moment. I think our witness is already a bit tired, the interpreters, myself as well. We will have a 20-minute break and we shall resume after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Cayley. We now had a break and I believe we've all recovered, or perhaps with a cup of coffee or something like that, and I think that we can now assume. So you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, from the 17th of July until the 21st of July, where did you find yourself?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the command of the Dutch Battalion, in the compound that were several hundred Dutch soldiers there and 27 Bosniaks. I already said that those were people who worked for UNPROFOR as interpreters, and some others who worked for MSF. MSF is an organisation called Medecins Sans Frontieres. So we were in Potocari in the compound between the 11th and the 21st of July, 1200 hours. At that time we left Potocari, we left Srebrenica, and across the Bosnian-Yugoslav border. We crossed into the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is, the first town across the border, Ljubovija, in the direction of Sabac, and then we moved on to Croatia. And on the 22nd, in the early morning hours, we arrived in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've just stated that the people who remained within the compound were members of the Dutch Battalion, various others, and some Bosniaks. Earlier you had stated that the man who accompanied you to the meeting on the 12th of July in the morning was Ibro Nuhanovic. You also stated in your evidence that Ibro subsequently disappeared. Can you tell the Court what you know happened to Ibro Nuhanovic and his family?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Ibro Nuhanovic, before the war, he was the manager of a timber processing company in the area of Srebrenica and Vlasenica. He had two sons, both students at the time, and his wife. On the 12th and 13th of July, he was a member of the Bosniak delegation. As you know, I already said that on the 12th and 13th of July, Bosniaks were deported in large numbers and people were separated, men and women, and so the Serb party requested that Ibro's wife and son be deported. Ibro knew about this request, but, as a parent and husband, according to what he said, he simply could not watch, could not suffer this separation, because after the first time they were to part company would not know anything about each other. So he joined his son and wife, and left. Several days later, when we arrived in Zagreb, we learned that neither he nor his wife or son had not reached the territory held at the time by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or even that his son, who survives, who is still alive, who is today alone and is suffering a great deal after he lost his father and mother and son [sic]. They looked for him -- he looked for them everywhere. He called even some people that his father and he knew before the war in the territory of the Republic of Srpska to ask them if they knew anything about his father or mother or his brother, but nobody could tell him anything definite. On a number of occasions I had the opportunity to talk to Ibro's son, who survived and who was in that group of 27 Bosniaks. And in those conversations I could see that today Ibro's son is an educated, an accomplished man. He works for IPTF, for UN forces, in the area of Tuzla. But he is a broken man, because he has no family and he is simply unable to start a normal life and live a life worthy of men like other people who did not suffer such losses as Hasim Nuhanovic, Ibro's son.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions of the witness, so I can now offer him for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Cayley. Now, Mr. Mandzic, you will answer the questions which counsel for the Defence, I believe Mr. Petrusic, or perhaps Mr. Visnjic -- no, Mr. Petrusic will have to ask of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Mandzic. I'm sorry, I did not get your surname right. Excuse me. My first question is whether you can tell us, Mr. Mandzic, something about how did the Serbs and Muslims live in the municipality of Srebrenica before the armed conflicts broke out.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you that. I am glad that you asked me that question. Before the war, Bosnia-Herzegovina was a multi-ethnic community with three constituent peoples, Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats, and other citizens. In such a multi-ethnic society life was indeed harmonious. There was mutual respect for religions or traditions of other peoples. There were no, and I repeat it again, there were no ethnic or religious obstacles, barriers between people. People socialised, people helped one another, people worked together. And Srebrenica was another such example of good multi-ethnic coexistence in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the territory of the formal Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In 1991, the first multi-party elections took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and a short time before that political parties had been set up and various political organisations. Until then, until the elections or after the elections, excuse me, after the elections, political authorities were to be constituted in the municipality of Srebrenica. You were in Srebrenica, as far as I could understand, when you gave your particulars to this Tribunal, so you were there. So could you tell us something about how these new authorities, how the new government was constituted after these first multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I've understood your question. The first multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the local ones for the municipality of Srebrenica, took place in the autumn of 1990, not in 1991. After the results of the elections were announced in Srebrenica, a multi-ethnic government was constituted on the basis of the census and the results of the elections. It needs to be pointed out that Bosniak political parties had the majority in the government and in the Municipal Assembly of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, you were a councilman in the municipality of Srebrenica, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not a councilman at that time, and you can see that in the Official Gazette of Srebrenica. You can see there how many councilmen were there in the municipal hall and who were those councilmen. I was not, but I was elected to the Municipal Assembly in 1997, and I'm now the mayor of the municipality and the councilman.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So those are the elections in 1997. In Srebrenica at that time, the Serbs were a minority, according to some sources. They accounted for some 25 to 30 per cent of the population.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At that time, they did not make up part of the municipal government, did they?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not correct. They were in the government. They were in the executive bodies of the Municipal Assembly. Let me explain this. After this multi-ethnic government and even before that we had multi-ethnic authorities when we still had a single-party system. We had authorities on the multi-ethnic basis and all the establishments and all the institutions, functions, and businesses, and everything else was governed by multi-ethnic principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But at that time, representatives, Muslim representatives in the Municipal Assembly, did they raise the question of the mayor of the municipality who was to be elected on the basis of that key which was widely applied in our country before and after those elections? So that was Zekic who was proposed to become ...

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me repeat it once again, that I was not a councilman. I did not have a seat in the Municipal Assembly at the time. But as far as I can remember, the president of the Municipal Assembly was to be elected from amongst the Bosniaks, that is, Bosniak political parties, because he needed -- he needed a majority in the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So can one say that in 1991 it already began some fermentation amongst the population, or, rather, among the political leaders and then this siphoned over to the population?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the multi-party system, there may have been some slight differences, but it did not find its reflection in the coexistence of the multi-ethnic community of Srebrenica. That is, people continued to live together harmoniously, to cohabit, and I can mention Skelani. In Skelani, Bosniak Serbs all the others, we went to school together, worked together, visited one another, were family friends and all that until 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Mandzic, why then did the Serb population leave Srebrenica in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They began to move out of Srebrenica then, yes, because in early spring and even before spring, I should say, it was in February that some local politicians, Serb politicians, began to request the constitution of a monoethnic Serb assembly and monoethnic Serb municipality of Skelani and some other monoethnic municipalities within the municipality of Srebrenica. I do not know whether this august court understands me. That is the territory of 529 kilometres square of the municipality of Srebrenica. There were some 38.000 inhabitants there. And some local Serb politicians in the municipality of Srebrenica wanted to partition the municipality of Srebrenica according to the ethnic principle, which simply could not be done because people were mixed. There were next-door neighbours you had in towns. In one and the same building you would have Serbs and Bosniaks and others, so that the majority of people there, and in my opinion, this was not really a very sensible request and could only deepen the misunderstanding between people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So Serbs were leaving Srebrenica at the time?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I can remember, a small or, rather, a large part of them did leave the town area itself, which had about 5.000 inhabitants. They were leaving the town by actually moving away their families to the towns such as Bajina Basta and other towns in Yugoslavia itself. We wanted to know why they were doing that, because no one was doing them any harm, but they would simply say, "Well, the times are somehow uncertain. We don't know what's going to happen. There might be a war," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What about the municipal authorities, the political structures who were in power at that time? Did they do anything to prevent this movement of population from the urban area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they did. First of all, it was the former president of the Municipal Assembly, Besim Besovic who acted at that time. He put a lot of personal effort in visiting various locations, seeing people, asking them not to panic, telling them that they had been living in the area together for hundreds of years and that they were capable of surmounting even this crisis, and he would tell them that there was no need for anyone to move away. However, I must stress that at that time, because the Serbs were leaving, some Bosniaks were leaving as well. Actually, it was the Bosniaks who had left the town area in March and April 1992. So, sir, let us be clear. The town of Srebrenica, in the month of April, was abandoned, first of all, by Bosniaks. It is true that part of Serbs had already moved their families away, but in the meantime, they had returned. However, the majority of Bosniaks who lived in the town area itself left the area at that time and, of course, they haven't come back to this very date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, at that time we see the establishment of armed forces in Potocari, for example, Sucaskin [phoen] And other villages, under the leadership the Naser Oric, Zulfo Tursunovic, and others. Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we should move back in time a little and see about the cause. It is true that the consequence was the formation of certain village guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Please allow me, Mr. Mandzic, to repeat the question. I think you should answer the question as it was put to you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that in early April paramilitary units of Arkan and some other units such as White Swans arrived in Bratunac and forced the Bosniak population to leave the town and surrounding areas, the same happened in Srebrenica where Arkan's and Sesan's units, with the connivance of certain Serbian politicians, entered the town itself and caused the Bosniak population to withdraw further into the interior part of the territory, into some remote villages. So those paramilitary units, most of which had come from the neighbouring country, that is, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, attacked the Bosniak villages. So as a result of that, as a consequence of that, the population were forced to defend themselves. And it is true that in certain villages, there were some village guards but which were not very well organised. Their task was mainly to protect the population from the exodus.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Then we see the formation of the protected area and an agreement on demilitarisation was also signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Will the interpreter say when there is a question and when there is an answer, because it is always the same voice and we don't know when it stops.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: It is the year of 1993. Relevant UN resolutions were passed and the area was declared a safe haven, and an agreement on the demilitarisation of the zone was signed between General Halilovic and General Mladic, General Halilovic being the Commander of the BH army. That enclave, the safe area of Srebrenica, was it ever truly demilitarised, Mr. Mandzic?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly it was. First of all, all of the heavy artillery was handed over to the Protection Forces in the presence, as far as I can remember and according to some other people who lived in the area, of some representatives of the VRS. An agreement was signed, and the heavy weapons were handed over. In addition to that, some light weaponry was also handed over. This could be seen by everybody who lived in the enclave. There used to be a huge pile of weapons next to the PTT building, and the light weaponry was mainly handed over to the UNPROFOR forces, but I don't know what they did with it, whether they destroyed it or what.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was the command of the 28th Division, which was commanded by Mr. Oric, quartered in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Legally speaking, I can say that it did not exist there at that time. In the enclave, there were no armed forces. In the month of September in 1995, I did see something happening in Tuzla. I know that the 28th Division was established there by General Delic. But it happened only several months after the takeover of the enclave by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The year of 1995?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1995 there was a review of the said division in Tuzla by the commander of the BH army, Rasim Delic. And let me mention one other fact. From January of 1993, I was no longer a member of the armed forces; I was only a teacher and I worked in the field of education.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to us, Mr. Mandzic, because I trust that you are familiar with the situation that was taking place after July 1995, and even before that. In the column that was formed in the village of Susnjari in the night between the 10th and 11th of July, there were at least 5.000 armed men. How did they end up there, bearing in mind the fact that the area had been demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for your question. First of all, I must tell that I was not present in the village of Susnjari at the time. I said that the demilitarisation of the enclave had been mostly finished, but, however, there were certain individuals who had their personal weapon licence for hunting rifles and some personal arms that they had kept as a souvenir in most of the cases. So one could see such individuals in Srebrenica, and elsewhere, and even groups of such people, but they were groups of civilians who had kept their personal weapons. But it was by no means, you know, hundreds of people. One could perhaps check the record of the police department in Srebrenica to see how many individuals indeed had weapon licences, and I think it would bring us to the number of, I don't know, somewhere between 500 and 1.000 individuals. Those were the people who had licences for their weapons, and I don't know anything about any other people with weapons. Those groups of people had kept weapons in order to protect their villages in such difficult situations. They were members of small, unorganised village guards which were not under any military control, properly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I can understand what you're saying, those weapons were -- it was possible to obtain those weapons through regular purchase, according to our legislation.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, you mean, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm referring to hunting weapons.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, not every citizen could obtain such weapons. I remember that there were requests, dozens of requests coming from, for example, a particular local community, but only 10 people would end up getting their licences.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What about automatic weapons, such as the infantry is using in the army? Such weapons were not kept. That is, I want to say that no licences could be issued for this type of weapons.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let us turn to the village of Slapovici and the 8th of July. Were there any armed formations in that village at that time?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is that on the 6th of July, units of the VRS ran over the checkpoint in Zeleni Jadar that was met by UNPROFOR forces, and they continued advancing in the direction of the village of Slapovici, where there were several thousands of refugees who had been displaced as early as in 1992 and 1993 from the areas such as the area of Bratunac, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, the Swedish Housing Project had several hundreds of flats at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And how many people were accommodated there?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my estimate, between two and three thousand. The then-representatives of the municipality of Srebrenica probably have reliable figures to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let us be precise. Those people at one point went from Slapovici to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there was a number of villages in the area where such columns were formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So you were referring to the columns of people that were formed in those villages?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Slapovici, and then also some neighbouring villages: Pusmulici and so on. The total figure would be somewhere over 6.000, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, turning to the first and the second meeting held on the 10th and the 11th of July in Bratunac, could you please tell us something more, more than what you said yesterday in your testimony, concerning the role and the participation of General Krstic in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that General Krstic, who is present here today and who was here yesterday, was sitting next to General Mladic. However, he did not say anything about the modalities regarding the population and how they should be taken care of or evacuated. And it was not an evacuation; it was a deportation, as we all know. General Krstic kept silent. Whether by doing so he approved of what Mladic was saying, that will be upon the Judges to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So you were present at the meeting, and on the following day, on the 12th of July, the meeting was attended by two other representatives of the Bosniak population as well. Could you now tell us who it was who actually conducted the negotiations; members of UNPROFOR -- we saw a video to that effect -- or yourself?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The negotiations were imposed on us by the Army of the Republika Srpska. They were imposed also on UNPROFOR. So the negotiations were mainly conducted, legally speaking, between the VRS and UNPROFOR. As for ourselves, we were merely a delegation which had the need and wish to express its concern about the situation, about the position in which more than 30.000 people had found themselves, about the humanitarian needs that they had at the time, and so on. However, at that meeting, if you remember what I said, I told General Mladic -- and it was quite a difficult moment; one had to muster a lot of courage to do so. I asked him, "Sir, whether, in view of the situation going on in the area of Srebrenica and Potocari, and bearing in mind the position of those 30.000 refugees and displaced persons, I wish to know whether relevant international authorities -- UNHCR, ICRC -- have been informed about the situation of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: As regards the situation in the base itself and the separation of males, was any distinction made in that respect? Could you be precise as to the criterion? Was it the working part of the population that was being separated or was it simply regardless of any criterion at all?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already stated before this Honourable Chamber, I saw women board buses, together with small children between 1 and 10 years of age, but I didn't see anybody else. And that is how I concluded that the units of the VRS had been separating menfolk from the rest of the population. Because mostly it was the elderly and the infirm who were in Potocari at that time, but there were also between 1.000 and 2.000 men who were there at that time. Let me just mention one example from a village of the Srebrenica municipality. There was a very old man who lived in my neighbourhood. He was 85 and he was there in a wheelchair. He was a very simple man, a peasant, a shepherd, who had spent his life as a peasant, and he is no longer alive, and there are hundreds of people whose fate was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, you talked about Colonel Nikolic who entered the base at one point. Do you have any knowledge as to the fact of his military position?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was he an officer from the infantry or did you perhaps come to a different conclusion? Did you perhaps think that he was an intelligence officer on an intelligence mission in the area? Because we have to bear in mind the fact that he was questioning those people, interrogating them.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not know which part of the army he belonged to. I can not say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: As regards the 12th of July, you said that units of the VRS were entering the area and you saw members of the VRS there at that time. Could you tell us if they had -- if they had some different insignia on their uniforms at that time?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already told Your Honours, I saw hundreds of soldiers. Some of them were wearing insignia, some did not. However, what I found rather surprising was the fact that there were hundreds of young soldiers who were there, who were there wearing uniforms, soldiers whom I had never seen in the area, and I believe I know the area very well. This is where I was born. I think that they would also have recognised me had they been from the area. But again, I must say that there were quite a few soldiers wearing no insignia at all, soldiers of the VRS, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was there any police? Could you make a distinction at that time between the military and the police?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not. I didn't see such insignia, whether they were the civilian or the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, the statement that was the subject of the last part of your examination-in-chief, could you tell us whether Major Franken, as one of the signatories of the statement, did he or anybody else request a new statement to be drafted? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and it's a very good question indeed. Looking with hindsight, it is true one could ask such a question. However, you have to bear in mind the situation at the time. There were about 30.000 refugees. Their deportation was imminent and it was to be to an unknown direction. Also because of the fact that on the 12th and the 13th of July, units of the VRS forcibly stopped a convoy of wounded. The convoy was stopped in Bratunac. And there were quite a few severely wounded people, civilians, in that convoy. Also, on the 17th of July, on that day, dozens of severely wounded persons had been gathered in Potocari as well. Some of them were still bleeding. I can remember that a Dutch Battalion medical officer, medical doctor, did perform certain very complex surgeries on those people. I also remember that during those days, soldiers of the VRS came to us, were checking on the population, intimidating the population. They were guarding the camp. And I know that Major Nikolic or, rather, Colonel Nikolic, as he was addressed to, I remember that they came personally to see about the people who had remained there. They wanted to know who they were, where they had come from, and what they were doing between 1992 and 1995. They inquired whether they knew Naser Oric and this other gentleman you mentioned. So a lot of pressure is being exerted on those people and myself as well. So we had no choice. The Serbian side wouldn't have it anyway. If they had wanted to have another declaration, another statement, they would have suggested that to us. They would have proposed another statement to be drafted which would reflect the effects on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Mandzic, the Serb delegation consisted only of Miroslav Deronjic at that point in time, on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And in the end, I'm quoting: "As regards the convoys escorted by the UN forces," end of quote. And this significantly changes the content, and that is why I'm asking you, and I do not doubt that there was fear, but if one adds a sentence, which, as I have said, changes the substance of this text, couldn't one do something, make an effort to draw up a new statement, bearing in mind that at that meeting there were no representatives of the army or police, there were only civilian representatives, rather, Miroslav Deronjic as the representative of the civilian authority in the municipality of Srebrenica. He was the only one present. So could you answer that question with yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement mentions other representatives of the military and civilian authority of the Republika Srpska, and the signatory, on behalf of all of them, is Deronjic. And I did see Deronjic in the Dutch battalion compound, but until that time, until that moment when Deronjic came to see Major Franken and when they invited me, they had been officers and soldiers of the VRS. From the place where we were sitting and where we signed that document, only five metres away were the guards of the Army of Republika Srpska. So that we had no say. We could have no saying in changing and rephrasing the document, with the exception of the last sentence in the statement that as far as the convoys escorted by UN -- by UNPROFOR forces were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And finally, do you -- are you aware that from Bratunac, from the hospital which was run by the International Red Cross, the wounded were evacuated, rather, Muslim wounded were transferred from Bratunac, from the hospital where they had been hospitalised, and were transported to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and with the Red Cross escort?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know many details about this, whether all those wounded managed to survive. Most of them, yes, I mean, those wounded. But it was only on the 17th of July that in the presence of some representatives of the International Committee of the Red Cross, but this -- there was, believe me, a much larger number of wounded, of sick, and we know nothing about their fate to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you too, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no questions for the witness on re-examination. I would simply ask to move a number of exhibits into evidence. They are Exhibit 40, which is the video of the second meeting in Bratunac; Exhibit 40A, "B," and "C," which are the English, French, and B/C/S translations of the transcript of that meeting; Exhibit 41, which is a still photograph of Colonel Karremans taken from that video; Exhibit 42, which is a still of Petar, a translator/interpreter; then there is Exhibit 43, which is the still of a VRS officer who the witness was unable to identify but did recognise being at the meeting; Exhibit 44, which is the still of General Mladic; Exhibit 45, which is the still of General Krstic; Exhibit 46, which is the still of a broken sign placed in front of the witness at the meeting. Then there is Exhibit 47, which composes of four parts, an English translation which is 47A; 47B, which is an English field translation; 47C, which is a French translation; and 47D, which is a B/C/S translation. And then finally Exhibit 48, which is the still of the Dutch Major, Major Boering. If I could apply for admission of all of those exhibits into evidence, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley. We shall continue in the presence of Mr. Mandzic, and we shall consider this at the end, but I have to ask the Defence. Do you have any objections against the admission of this evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These exhibits will be admitted. Now I shall give the floor to my colleagues to see if they have any questions. Judge Riad, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning, Mr. Mandzic.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I would like you to give me some more precision about what you have been telling us. First concerning the meeting in the Fontana Hotel, which you talked about with the Prosecutor and with Defence counsel, the meeting of the 12th of July at 10.00. You mentioned that General Krstic was sitting next to General Mladic and that he was silent. Was there any other manifestation in that meeting, whether from the side of General Krstic or the others, of approval of this or disapproval or threat or anything, or were they just silent witnesses. Could they have expressed anything in the presence of Mladic, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, when I speak about the second meeting which took place on the 12th of July, 1995 in the Fontana Hotel, yes, indeed, next to General Mladic was General Krstic. General Krstic and other officers representing the command of the Army of Republika Srpska were not adding anything to what General Mladic was saying. When he would say something -- I mean, General Mladic, when General Mladic turned to me and said, "Nesib, everything is in your hands. You can survive or you can vanish as people from the face of the earth because God Almighty has given us life and given us room to leave in peace, so it is logical that the survivability of a community, of a people is determined, decided by the Maker," and the other side of General Mladic then says, "Or you may vanish," none of the military representatives of the Army of Republika Srpska or the civilian authorities reacted to that.
