They went along with the General's idea that a local community might or the population might vanish, and that is -- that particular thing which instilled fear in the Bosniak delegation, in us, all along those days we felt this tremendous pressure to begin with because of the presence of all those officers and soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska, but we were also under tremendous psychological pressure which was created by the encirclement and by the creation of a ghetto, I have to put it that way, in this small area in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Then I just gathered you repeated several times the word "vanish." You understood from it clearly that it was to vanish from this planet, from this world, or to vanish from Srebrenica or Bosnia? Was it vanishing in the meaning of extermination, in your opinion, or -- clearly was it extermination?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That word I understood meant "to vanish"; the disappearance, the end of life of all those people, their execution. Somebody was depriving, was taking away their right to life. And that kind of power was then with the Army of Republika Srpska, their power, and General Mladic put it in so many words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: How many were the other officers with General Mladic, and what was their rank, if you know, of General Krstic, or his importance in this group of Mladic?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that on the first night, I mean the 11th of July, sometime around 11.00 at night, General Mladic introduced all the officers who were present, the officers of the Army of Republika Srpska; first, General Krstic, and he introduced him as a corps commander. At that time I was slightly taken aback that General Krstic was the corps commander, to begin with, because listening from time to time to radio news, and we had difficulty in hearing that in Srebrenica, while we lived in the enclave, because all the radio transmission equipment had been destroyed around us and the signal was very weak. But in 1993, 1994, the commander of the corps of the Drina Corps was General Zivanovic. And most of the Bosniaks and Serbs in the area, in the municipalities of Srebrenica and Bratunac, knew him, because he came -- he was born in that area, from the boundary between Srebrenica, Bratunac municipalities, and so I was quite surprised to hear that General Krstic was the commander of that corps. But General Krstic, and I repeat that, did not amplify on what General Mladic was saying, nor did he say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I gather from what you said that General Krstic replaced Zivanovic, who you thought or you knew was the corps commander. Was that related a little bit to what was preceding the events which happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not think it had any effect. I do not think it really mattered who was the corps commander. They simply expected General Zivanovic to be that, because he came from that area, from the municipality of Srebrenica. I did not know that General Krstic had replaced him. But I doubt that anything would have happened differently. If the plan was to take the Srebrenica -- or rather, their plan was to take the enclave and to expel and to separate the male population, and other physical and psychological barriers that the civilian population was confronted with in those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: A corps commander means that he will be one giving the orders?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslav Army, that is, in the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, I served the army in 1981, 1982, and at that time a corps commander, from what I knew, was also a member of the Main Staff, that is, the second in command to the commander of the armed forces. And in his area of responsibility, the authority covered by the units subordinate to him. He used to be the man who would have complete control and therefore responsible for the conduct of whatever operations, naturally, I assume, while informing, while notifying the Main Staff about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned something about these people, the VRS soldiers, whom you never saw before -- some of them were young -- and they had no insignia and they had a different accent. Now, you being about more or less -- I think you are a man of culture and you know the accents a little bit perhaps of the area. What accent did they have? From which part, do you think?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I completed my secondary education in Belgrade and I worked there for about a year and a half after I matriculated from the secondary school. So I know the Ekavian dialect, such as is spoken by Counsel Petrusic. In Serbia most people will use Ekavian dialect. In Bosnia-Herzegovina or, specifically, the north-eastern Bosnia, they will speak Ijekavian dialect. But at that time I could, as I said, I could hear young soldiers, whom I did not know, well uniformed, clean-shaven, very tidy, very neat, who were selectively torching houses in the Potocari area, I assume having received orders to that effect, and their speech varied. Some of them, they spoke Ijekavian dialect, or there was a mixture of the two dialects, of the Ekavian and Ijekavian, and, as far as I remember, an Ekavian speech, but different from the one spoken by those who live in west Serbia. It sounded more like the speech, like the dialect of Vojvodina and Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you are finished? Good. Now, another question concerning the list which was given to Major Franken. It was the list of 239 men which apparently disappeared, if I understood rightly. And he told you he would put it in his trousers and nobody would take it. Have you an idea of the future, what happened to this list?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I spent months trying to locate this list of 239 men, and Ibro Nuhanovic's son was also trying to trace it. I told you that Ibro Nuhanovic was a member of the Bosnian delegation and we just do not know what happened to him. And it was only through some journalists who came from Western Europe to Bosnia-Herzegovina that Hasan Nuhanovic was able to get that list, and he showed me and I saw it and I also have it. I wrote it in my own hand. But it was only several months later, perhaps four or five months later I was able to see it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But during these months you don't know what happened to it, in whose hands it was?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in whose hands it was. We made some guesses that perhaps the Dutch battalion commander, or perhaps his deputy, Major Franken, had given it to the UNPROFOR command for former Yugoslavia, which I believe was headquartered in Zagreb. But we as individuals could not get the list, because there were some -- it was said that the list, or rather a copy of that list with 239 names could be given only to some organisations, and like that. But I was concerned. I was really worried. I really hoped that the list would not be destroyed and that we would lose any trace of existence of those men. But Mr. President, Your Honours, when one -- when I leafed through that list before I left Bosnia for The Hague and for this august institution, I went through that list and I felt a lump in my throat, because those people are no more. And the world watched quietly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Some people refused to have their names on the list. Are they also no more, or perhaps some of them are still around?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may just a minute. May I have just a minute? I need to calm down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Sorry. I can stop my questions.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but, you know, they were all my fellow townsmen. I can. I can. Yes, I'm all right now. I'm all right now. Your Honours, there were also some men of different ages, even those of 80 and over, who in such a dramatic situation refused to be included in the list, fearing that the list might fall into the hands of the Army of Republika Srpska. And they thought, well, if they don't know my name, then who he is and what he is, perhaps it will make it easier through the checkpoints of the Army of Republika Srpska. Lamentably, that is not what happened. Yes, you may go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned, you answered the Defence counsel that Serbs started leaving Srebrenica in 1992. There was something -- I think 5.000, I don't -- something of that count, and they said the times are somehow uncertain, this is why they left, because, according to you, there was no mistreatment, there was no threat. How -- I mean, were there some rumours, or perhaps some information, now that you effectively received, they received, to know what was going to happen, and that it was safer to go out? Why did they leave, if there was no threat or no mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mentioned, I don't know how it was translated, that prior to the war in 1992, approximately 38.000 people lived in the territory of the Srebrenica municipality. In the town itself, there were about 5.000 people, and more than 32.000 lived outside the town area, and they lived in the so-called local communes. So as far as the town area is concerned there were about 1.500 to 2.000 Serbs. So the Bosniaks were the majority in the town as well. In the spring, in April of 1992, on the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in neighbouring towns on the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, such as Bajina, Basta, Ljubovija, military units were located on those borders, and there was a heavy concentration of troops on those borders, troops belonging to the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Several months earlier that country put a ban on the import of food stuffs for the population in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Since both Bosniaks and Serbs regularly had to cross over that border prior to the conflict, they had an opportunity to see armed units in the area, and according to what they said, those units made it perfectly clear that they would be coming to Bosnia to protect Serbs, as they put it. Again, I must say, and I'm speaking the truth, and nothing but the truth, that before the month of April, in the territory of the Bratunac and Srebrenica municipalities, there had been no armed forces, either of Bosniaks or Serbs. That was the case until mid-April, and until that time they lived together, they worked together, their children went to school together. But at one point in time, paramilitary units entered the area from the republic of Yugoslavia. I'm referring first of all to the units of Arkan. They came to Bratunac. And this caused panic amongst the population. And at that moment Srebrenica was being abandoned both by Bosniaks and Serbs, together, if I may put it that way. Serbs were mostly moving their families away into the neighbouring towns in Serbia. Bosniaks were leaving to major Bosniak centres such as Tuzla, for example, and the towns in that area. The result of that situation in the territory of the Srebrenica municipality was such that as early as the 17th of April, I think, paramilitary units, together with certain local Serbian politicians who were hard-liners and were supported by certain members of their population, they entered the town of Srebrenica. There were no Bosniaks in the town area itself at the time. They had fled, in the meantime, out of fear. Several elderly Bosniaks had remained, of course. But at that moment, the paramilitary units entered the town, and in late April and early May, several people, several elderly people, were killed by the members of those paramilitary units. The victims were old and infirm Bosniaks. And let us not be confused about that. In April of that year, citizens of both ethnic groups were leaving Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I think I understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, you referred, in your earlier testimony, to the fact that there were about 5.000 people in the UN Compound before the evacuation and maybe 15.000 to 20.000 people were outside the compound in the neighbouring streets, congregated, milling around. I have two questions. One is: You also testified, and I think we saw a video of Colonel Karremans, who said basically the vast majority of the evacuees were women and children or maybe the elderly or the sick. Is that true of the group that was outside the compound, the 15.000 to 20.000, as well as those that were inside, or were there considerably greater proportion of men in the group outside the compound?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for your question, Your Honour. At the base itself, at the camp, approximately 5.000 people had found shelter. However, outside the camp there were no 15.000 or 20.000 people but probably more than 25.000 people. I think that their situation was far worse than the situation of the people who had gathered in the camp two or three days before. They had no water. They had no toilet facilities. They had no food. On the other hand, they were being attacked by the VRS units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand that from your prior testimony. My question specifically was though: In that 25.000 people outside, were they mostly women and children too or were they more a mixture of men? From the photographs one would see many men there, but it was a greater percentage of men in the outside group than of the inside group? Is that right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that group, in that mass of 25.000 people, there were mostly women and children, but to answer specifically that question as regards the male population between 18 years of age and 60, I think that there were more of them outside than inside the camp. And proportionally speaking, there were, of course, much more people outside the camp than within the compound itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question along the same lines is: When the evacuation began, were the people outside the compound the ones -- the 25.000 that you talked about, were they put on buses or were the people inside the compound put on buses first and, later on, what happened to that group outside the compound once the evacuation began?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm using the word "deportation." I felt it on my own skin. Began on the 12th of July, in the early afternoon hours. The first to be put on buses were persons standing outside the camp, and then it was only later on, in the afternoon hours of the 13th of July, that the persons inside the camp were being put on buses, were being deported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, on the night of the 11th in the Fontana Hotel, the first meeting that you went to and of which we saw a video, General Mladic said several times words to the effect of, "Get your people to lay down their arms if they want to survive. Survival is in your hands. Bring me a delegation that can produce people who will lay down their arms if you want to preserve the population." Now, at that point, as you have testified and others as well, the people in the compound and outside of the compound were mainly women and children. The column that was going to Tuzla had already left, is that not right? It left from a neighbouring village. So how did you understand General Mladic's ultimatum to be? If you had wanted to accede to it, what could you have done? The people with the arms had already left, as I understand it, and begun to march towards Tuzla on their own, and the people that were left in the compound were largely women and children. So how did you -- when he talked about "survive or vanish" or "lay down your arms," what do you think he wanted you to do?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember very well what General Mladic said and how he threatened us. He said, "Lay down your weapons and you can either survive or vanish." It was difficult to understand such a request, because we were simply representatives of the displaced population. We were not representatives of any armed force. However, General Mladic persisted in his request that we should lay our weapons, and nobody had anything -- nobody amongst the population that gathered there. So I realised it was a kind of psychological pressure, and I feared the worst for that population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: When you convened the next morning with your three-person delegation, did General Mladic bring that up again? You didn't testify too much about what was happening on the morning of the 12th. Did he again say, "Well, here's your delegation. I want you to tell me you'll lay down your arms and everything will be all right," or did he just drop that subject altogether on the morning of the 12th meeting?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, to the best of my recollection, on the following day, on the 12th of July, General Mladic reiterated the request to our delegation. He said, "Lay down your weapons," and again, as far as I can remember, he said that, "Whoever lays down his weapons, I, as a General and a human being, can guarantee there would be no problems, would have no problems. Our objective is not to harm the Muslim population, and we will enable every single individual, regardless of age and sex, to choose the place where he or she wants live."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did anyone in your delegation ask him or suggest to him that you didn't have a population with arms, you just had some women and children and some elderly and infirm displaced persons, there was no way to get them to lay down arms that they didn't have?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. This was done firstly by Mrs. Camila Omanovic, as a member of our delegation. She said, "Well, sir, we have nothing to do with those who took to the woods, who may have weapons with them. What we have here are refugees, displaced persons without any food, water, medicine, clothing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Am I correct that in both the 11th meeting in the evening and the 12th meeting there was a film crew filming this, or was it only the night of the 11th that General Mladic had a film crew who was filming the whole thing? Were they on the 12th or were they on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 11th and the 12th of July, the film crew was there, and they also came to Potocari on the 13th of July. I could see them there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My last question deals with the document that we talked about that was signed on the 17th. You went over, with Mr. Cayley, some of the statements that you said were not correct, were inaccurate. Let me point your direction to one of them that you did not discuss, to get your opinion on that. It is the one -- the third from the bottom which says: "It was agreed that we could choose where we wanted to go. We decided that the entire civilian population move out of the enclave and be evacuated to the territory of Kladanj." Now, can you tell me your opinion on whether that was an accurate statement that "we," whoever "we" is, "decided that the entire civilian population would move out"?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not an accurate statement, Your Honour. Between the 6th and the 11th of July, units of the VRS forced about 40.000 strong population of the area to leave their homes, to abandon their estates, their belongings, everything they had. Most of them found themselves in Potocari; that is, they were directed by VRS units to that particular location because of the fire that was being opened. The population was pushed up to Potocari by VRS units. On the 12th and the 13th of July, VRS units encircled the area and started entering the group of people. Then they began separating the population according to their age and sex. They started putting people on buses. We are the kind of people that cannot easily accept departure from our homes and separation. Every single change, every move to another town, another city is very difficult to us, let alone deportation. So this statement is by no means true and does not reflect the real situation. If there had been any understanding on the part of VRS units, if they had withdrawn at least here at the boundaries of the demilitarised area, everybody, all of the population, would have come back. I apologise, Your Honour, but I have to say that we had been living as refugees for years. We have been living as refugees for years, and we're trying to go back but this is very difficult. Before the war, we, and I refer to both Bosniaks and Serbs, used to have a good life there. We had our houses there, we had good salaries. There were no homeless people. We had, you know, more houses than families. There are figures that can testify to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: At the time of this statement, July 17th, 1995, did any Serbians still live -- any Serb civilians still live in Srebrenica? I know you talked a great deal and told us a great deal about how the Bosniaks and the Serbs, starting in April, had begun to leave, but were there any Serbian civilians left in Srebrenica in July?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean before the capturing of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: At the time of the Potocari -- no, after the capturing. At the time of the Potocari evacuation, were there any Serbians still resident, living in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since 1992, that is, May 1992 until July 1995, there had been a small group of Serbian citizens, mostly elderly people. And on that day, on the 11th of July when this massive persecution occurred of the members of the Bosniak community, that small group of Serbian residents remained. And I can say that because I work in Srebrenica, that most of them still live there and work there, and they still hoped that we would come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But on the other -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as I can see, we have been working for one and a half hours, and this has been quite an ordeal for our interpreters. I'm in a bit of a quandary here. I have questions myself, but it wouldn't make much sense to bring back the witness after the recess. Would you be so kind as to give us another 10 minutes? I will try and be very brief in my questions. Very well. Thank you very much. Mr. Mandzic, I have three questions for you, and I will try to be as brief as possible, and I should also ask you to answer with the same concern in mind. I'm interested in reasons of the signature on this statement as it was presented to you. Did they explain to you any reasons for the signing of the statement?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is stated here is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry to interrupt you. I would like to know if the persons who produced this document told you, "You're going to sign it because so-and-so."

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were all very well aware of the fact that in Bratunac, which was a town controlled by the VRS, that several dozens of wounded persons had been kept, that in Potocari there was still a number, that is, several dozens of severely wounded persons, including women and children, and we also knew that at the time there were 27 healthy persons, who also wanted to survive, still there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But what you're telling me are your own reasons, the reasons you perceived as being such. What I'm interested in is what Mr. Deronjic told you. Did he explain anything? Did he tell you why you had to sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. He did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were aware of the situation. You knew what would happen, and you felt that you had to sign this document. Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The fate of probably 80 or 100 Bosniaks depended on our signature and also the fate of the soldiers of the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Mandzic. You have spoken about that. Thank you very much. We are little pressed for time. I have one other question in respect of this document. You signed a declaration, a statement, in your language, and you also signed a copy in English. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, did you understand English?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Still on the same document. In most of the sentences the plural is used in this document. It says, "we," "our civilian population," and so on and so forth, but at one point it is stated: "After the agreement was reached, I claim that the evacuation of the civilian population of the Srebrenica enclave was carried out absolutely correctly," and so on. I'm interested to know who was the person who was speaking. Who used this particular expression "I claim"?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no Bosniak delegation, properly speaking, on the 13th of the July. Mr. Nuhanovic, with his family, had left; that is, we didn't know anything about him. Mrs. Camila Omanovic had a nervous breakdown because soldiers of the VRS had entered the area. So they knew very well about the whereabouts of the members of the Bosniak delegation. So I was the only one who was capable of following the situation. I was trying to record everything but, of course, I wasn't in the position to record everything because I feared that whatever I write might end up in the hands of the Serb army. So the only person they could count upon was myself, and I was the one who had to understand the situation of those people, and their fate depended on this understanding of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this expression "I claim," first person singular, refers to you?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but it is not mine, properly speaking, because I was not the drafter of this statement, and the statement did not reflect the facts. It was prepared in advance, and it was merely an ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mandzic, you probably read this document several times, and you probably read it more than I did. If you have a look at it, all we have throughout the document is the first person plural, "we", "our population," and so on and so forth. But there is one paragraph, one single paragraph where the wording used is "I claim." What I'm trying to understand is who it was who said, "I" and who it was who used the expression "we" and "our." Are you in a position to explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, and I, probably referred to a representative of the civilian government of Republika Srpska. In this document, where it is stated "I claim," I do not claim anything, because I was not the drafter of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if I can use the expression, there is some kind of schizophrenia in this document. We have two persons speaking at the same time. At any rate, we will see later on how this problem can be resolved.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, in this document the drafter of the document used the word "I" conscientiously. Two other members of the delegation, Nuhanovic, for example, had been taken away. He had probably been killed in the meantime. Camila Omanovic had had a nervous breakdown. In the previous sentences the persons are speaking -- are used in plural. Probably several persons are needed to have a proper agreement, but I was the only one who was there, so the drafter of this particular statement had all the necessary knowledge about our situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Another question which I have concerns the presence of General Krstic. We know that he was present at two meetings in Bratunac on the 10th and on the 11th. Did you see him again after those two meetings?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Krstic, I never saw him before the 11th of July. The only time I saw him was on the 11th and the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Another question. Mr. Mandzic, it is Exhibit 40A, and this is the transcript of a video, which I wish to read to you. General Mladic asks you, "Are you a teacher?" And you say, "Yes, I was this morning, but I don't know for how long." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic put a question to me: what was my profession and what had I done before the war and while living in the enclave. And I told him that before the war I was a teacher also in the enclave in 1994, 1995, that I was a teacher and school principal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Mandzic. Will you please try to answer my question directly. General Mladic asked you, "Are you a teacher?" And you said, "Yes, I am. I was one this morning, but I do not know for how long yet." And Mladic then goes on, "What school did you come from?" And you say, "The electrical engineering." My question is, what did you mean when you said, "I was this morning, but I don't know for how long yet." So this is my question. Would you please try to answer it directly.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know if I would live to see another day or not, because the enclave had been taken, its population expelled, and I could see that the Bosnian Serb army was treating the Bosnian population ruthlessly, so I simply realised that I could expect the worst.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have finished. I do not have any more questions at the moment. So you answered the questions of the counsel for the Prosecution, the counsel for the Defence, the Judges. Is there anything that you should like to say and were not asked about? If there is something that you should like to tell us, you can do so now.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, about life in Srebrenica between 1992 and 1995, about the suffering of the population, the expulsion, and so on and so forth, one could go on and on. But what I should like to emphasise, and it goes beyond this institution, is how to overcome the effects. In the first place, I have in mind tens of thousands of expelled who live in Tuzla, Sarajevo, and dozens of other places around the Federation, and most of them have said that they would like to go back to their homes. But for political and other barriers, people are not returning. And they live now as second-rate citizens. They suffer because their life is not worthy of man. But I do know that that is not a subject that is dealt by this Tribunal. But any advice, any recommendation that you might have, I would think would be of great help to other institutions who are responsible for trying to resolve the problem of refugees and displacement as soon as possible, to help those people go back home and live life worthy of human beings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Mandzic. We have finished. You have told us about your suffering. Thank you. You showed great courage in coming and testifying here. You have also given evidence of your spirit of tolerance. I believe I speak in the name of my colleagues when I tell you that we all wish you a happy return to your home. Yes, those places were witness to suffering, but they should also be witness to tolerance and peace. Injustice, wherever, shall always be a threat to everybody. Now I believe I must make it up to everybody, and especially the interpreters, and we shall make a half-an-hour break now and we'll resume after the break with another witness. Half an hour, therefore. Thank you and farewell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now we have also had the opportunity of enjoying this great weather, and I believe the interpreters did the same thing, but now I think it is time to resume. Mr. Cayley, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just a point that relates to the document with which you were concerned, which is Exhibit 47, and we've been notified by the translation and interpretation unit that there is, in fact, a mistake in the French translation in the final paragraph. In the English translation -- this is the final paragraph on page 1 of the document: "After the agreement was reached, I claim." That is what it states in the English translation, and apparently the verb used in the French translation is wrong, and is not a correct translation of the original version in B/C/S. Please don't ask me the details. Being an Englishman, I'm embarrassingly unilingual, so I don't want to get involved in arguments over what it should be but, nevertheless, we're informed it's wrong and a corrected version will be produced, which we will submit to the Court tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because if one reads the French version, "exiger," "I demand it," then the English version should say, "I claimed." But my question was not to find out about the correct tense but whether it was singular or plural. But we shall wait for the amended version to see the result. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think that the tense is actually correct in terms of -- in fact, not that you refer to the tense, whether the word "I" or "we" was used. But from my own interpretation of this document, if you go to the second paragraph, it actually states, "The representatives from our side were Camila Purkovic, Ibro Nuhanovic, and myself Nesib Mandzic." Now, I'm obviously not really in a position to really argue the matter before you, Mr. President. Perhaps now is not the proper time. But I think the document does actually make it clear that he was signing as an individual on behalf of two people that were not present, and that is why the document was drafted in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Be that as it may, I do not usually follow the French translation. Now that I did have the French translation, we have a problem, but I will still want to have French translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I believe that "claim" is not "exiger" in French. "Exiger" is stronger than "claim," but there are more greater authorities than me. "Claim" could be "required" or even "wanted," but "exiger" is too strong. So perhaps you have to check that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You're asking somebody who is not an authority, Judge Riad, but that is certainly the explanation that has been given to me, that "exiger" is a much stronger term. I think it means "request" rather than "claim." It's "request" rather than "affirmation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but we are not now to go into the review of the translation, but we do work indeed under very difficult conditions. These cases are very difficult. We all work under very difficult conditions and, therefore, it is absolutely requisite that we maintain good communication. However, I should like also to apologise to the interpreters, but I also wish to say that we have only a certain concentration, capacity, and after a certain time, of course, it simply declines, after a certain period of time. So perhaps we should try to keep the -- to discuss sets of questions, entities of questions separately, not to go to one or two things. I also think that 50 minutes would be -- 50 minutes is decided to be a good period of time for children, during which they can hold their concentration. For the adults it's closer to an hour, 1 hour and 10. After that, they lose the concentration. So we say that 1 hour and 10 minutes is a good time, and perhaps 1 hour and 20. After that we should make a break because, otherwise, I'm afraid it might damage the communication, because somebody is about to finish something and then we get into 1 hour and 10 minutes, 1 hour and 20 minutes. I believe that both parties can, in such a case, take initiative, make a sign, for instance, this international sign, I believe everybody shows that, and say, "Let us make a break because the powers of concentration are rapidly declining." So we should bear in mind the time and our powers of concentration. Thank you very much for this. Now I think we are ready for the next witness. I see that it will be Mr. Harmon who will -- tell us, you are omniscient, you are all-knowing, Mr. Harmon, so will you tell us what we're going to do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, our next witness is Mrs. Camila Omanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mrs. Omanovic. Did you hear me? Would you stand up and remaining standing just for a short while, please. Madam, you will now read the solemn declaration which you will be given by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may take your seat now. Just make yourself comfortable. Thank you for coming here to testify, Mrs. Omanovic, to give your evidence before the International Criminal Tribunal. You will now answer questions which the Prosecution, Mr. Harmon, will ask of you. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Omanovic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you spell your last name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: O-m-a-n-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you spell your first name for the record?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: C-a-m-i-l-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 15th of April, 1953, in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm not getting a translation, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We'll continue, Mrs. Omanovic. Could you tell the Judges about your educational background, please?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: I completed my elementary and secondary education in Srebrenica. Then I enrolled in university in Tuzla, and I completed the first stage of the faculty of economics, and I came back to Srebrenica and found a job there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you born in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, I'm sorry, but I cannot see on the transcript the date of birth of Mrs. Camila Omanovic. Perhaps you could ask her to repeat it, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mrs. Omanovic, could you repeat your date of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Srebrenica on the 15th of April, 1953.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges when you were married?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the 10th of February, 1977. That is when I married Ahmet Omanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: I had two children, Dzermina Omanovic, born on the 28th of October, 1977; and Dzermin Omanovic, born in 1981, on the 25th of December. My daughter also married in Srebrenica, and she gave birth to a child in 1985, in March of 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In 1985 or in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So at the time of the events that you're going to be describing to the Judges, you had a grandchild; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My grandchild was born on the 10th of March, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you continue to work in the area of Srebrenica or Potocari after your marriage?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked in Srebrenica and Potocari throughout my life there, both my husband and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say that you're quite familiar with the area of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: I know the area of Potocari quite well because from 1996 my husband worked there, and besides, that is my native country, so I do know Potocari very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mrs. Omanovic, let me ask you one last question about your background. Are you, by faith, a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: I am a Muslim by faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And was your husband Ahmet likewise, by faith, a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my husband Ahmet was also a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Omanovic, I'd like to focus your attention on the 10th of July, 1995, and I'd like to ask you to tell the Judges where you were on that date.

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was, on that day, in my brother's house, Zulfo Turkovic. His house is at the exit from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, can you see the large map that's to your right? Could you take a pointer and point to the general location where your brother's house was located?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was here approximately [indicated].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the record is perfectly clear, the witness has pointed south of the town of Srebrenica, near the hairpin turn indicated below the town of Srebrenica. You may resume your seat. Who was with you --

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's quite all right Mrs. Omanovic. Who was with you at your brother's house on the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: The 10th of July in my brother's house were my husband and my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On that date, did something unusual happen? Can you describe to the Court what it was and what you did in reaction to it?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: That day there was a lot of gunfire around my brother's house. As I came out of -- came out of the house onto the terrace and was engaged in some everyday chores, I could see very many people loaded with luggage moving towards the town, and I didn't pay much attention to it because the day before that I had sent my daughter and my son into town to my daughter's flat, and my husband and my brother and I stayed in the house. I had livestock which we had brought during the war merely to survive. There was a lot of gunfire around us, but it was at a distance, and we'd already become immune to it and were not paying much attention. But at a certain point I looked through the window, across the river, the house there. I saw a group of people who were carrying that luggage and were standing below the terrace and indicating or mimicking that fire was coming from above the house. Then I looked to the other side and saw thousands of bullets hitting the facade of my brother's house. My brother jumped across the terrace and made his way from one house to another to go there. My husband and I did not jump from the terrace. We ran down the stairs to the next-door house and thus we came with very many people who were coming from all the houses, and we all headed towards the town. The gunfire was gaining momentum, and I think it came from all the weapons, from artillery, from infantry, and shells and bullets were falling all around us. We, however, managed to get to the town, and the gunfire then stopped. I mean, there was some sporadic, intermittent fire, one could hear it in the town, but it was not as intensive as on the periphery. That night I spent with my daughter and grandchild, and lots of people who got there who were all rallied in the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to speak slower, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You've been asked by the interpretation booth if you could just speak a little slower. Now, let me focus your attention on the following day, the 11th of July. Tell the Judges what you did.

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 11th I went back to Petrica -- that is where my brother's house is -- because the livestock had to be fed. And also the laundry, the diapers of my grandchild, were still drying on the clothesline behind the house. And my husband and I decided to go early in the morning and go back to my brother's house. And that is what we did. We followed the bank of the river and we reached the house and there was no gunfire. And on our way we met various people, neighbours, who said because Srebrenica is in a valley, in a hollow, and they said that a bullet would be fired from time to time by snipers. But we got to the house, we fed the livestock, we cut off the clothesline and all the diapers fell down, and we came out. We just picked it up in a hurry and went back to our daughter's. And there was a lull until about afternoon and then hell broke loose, because gunfire came from all sides, from all possible weapons. And people again, with all that luggage, they headed for Potocari. And we somehow gathered all around the petrol pump which was near the UN base, which was by the petrol station near Bratunac. And there were very many people there, women, children, and just whatever they happened to be wearing. They had children on their shoulders or some small belongings. They were milling about, screaming, because shells were falling from all over. The road was so narrow that all those people simply could not fit in, fit onto the road, and there were several trucks which tried to take people to Potocari, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for just a minute, Mrs. Omanovic. Were you with your husband around noon on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was with my husband, and the whole family was there together. And then we parted our ways at the petrol station. He went towards Kazani. All the men, all the men over 13, headed for it. Somehow a selection started, and they headed off towards the Kazani and we headed for Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, what was the date of birth of your husband?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: My husband was born in Mostar on the 10th of July, 1948.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, were there -- at this gas station, were there a lot of people who went in a different direction other than Potocari?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, very many people went in the other direction who did not go to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, were the people who went in the direction other than Potocari, were they mostly men and boys, or were there some women involved in that particular group as well?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: Men, by and large, but there was an occasional women amongst them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did some of these men in this group by the gas station have guns?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: Some of them -- some of the men did have weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did your husband have a gun?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: My husband did not have a weapon. A month before that he had been operated on and felt -- and was unwell. But he nevertheless started for the forest, because rumours spread that if he fell into the Serb hands, that he would be maltreated, and he would not allow that, and so he went to the forest with other men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, was the 11th of July, 1995 the last time you saw your husband alive?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: That was the last time I saw him; never again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mrs. Omanovic, there should be some tissues to your left. Mrs. Omanovic, in which direction did you proceed, and with whom did you proceed in that direction?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: With my daughter, son, and grandchild, I started to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how old was your son at the time and how old was your daughter and grandchild?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: My grandchild was 4 months old, my daughter was 17, and my son 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Judges the environment as people fled toward Potocari; how many people there were, what the conditions were like, the state of mind of the people who were fleeing from Srebrenica to Potocari was like?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a huge crowd; several thousand women, children, and old people and babies, and they all had one thing in mind: to escape, to flee to the UN base in Potocari. Because we believed that if we did reach that, that we would be saved. Everybody was in a hurry. Everybody was carrying their belongings, babies. Women were crying, screaming. It was such a huge throng of panicking people with only one thing in mind: Let's get to Potocari as quickly as possible. If we get there, we'll be all right. And under such conditions, gunfire came from all sides. Thousands and thousands of bullets, and a swarm of bees all around buzzing all the time, and every now and then shells were fired at this crowd. And in all this confusion somebody lost his belongings, somebody a piece of bread. An old woman who could not manage in this crowd fell. And APC, if it came across a body put aside, they would simply be collected, put on the APC. And they were simply telling us, "Hurry, hurry." I was somewhere in the rear of this column and I had all my luggage and the baby's luggage in the pram. My daughter took the baby and started for Potocari. But there were so many remains of clothes and personal affairs on the road that you couldn't really push the pram really to reach Potocari, but somehow we covered those five kilometres, and that was really -- that was really sheer horror.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mrs. Omanovic, did all the people who fled from Srebrenica to Potocari go on foot or were some people taken in UN vehicles?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: Some of the people were taken in a UN vehicles; however, not everybody could be transported in that way. The first group of people, who was the closest to the UN base, they were put on the trucks and they were crowded. But there was a lot of panic going on, because everybody wanted to board those trucks at the same time. They were clinging on the trucks because they believed, they hoped, that they would be safe if they reached the area in time. So everybody rushed towards those trucks. There were lots of people coming from all sides. They were trying to get hold of the truck, and the trucks had to leave before everybody was on board, and there were lots of people actually clinging from those trucks as they were leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would now like to show a film. It's about seven minutes long. It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 50. And if we could have the lights dimmed and Prosecutor's Exhibit 50 shown. And this film, Mr. President and Your Honours, is in the UN compound in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mrs. Omanovic, do these images that we've been looking at for the last few minutes accurately depict the condition of the refugees as you recall them?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they do. This is exactly how it happened. Only this is just a small excerpt. You have to imagine thousands and thousands of more people coming in; you have to imagine all those voices. The whole thing has to be magnified. This is only one truck that we saw. Now, you have to imagine several thousands of people and the noise being much louder, and you also have to bear in mind that we kept hearing fire and the shells that were falling all around us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were the weather conditions like on the 11th of July in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a very warm day. It was very hot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Potocari, where did you go specifically?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: Together with my family, I went to the compound of the Zinc Factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, could I, with the assistance of the usher, have Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/2 placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mrs. Omanovic, I've shown you this exhibit before. I'm going to ask you to point out on Prosecutor's 5/2 the location of the Zinc Factory and orient the Judges to other locations that will be relevant to your testimony.

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: On the first day, that is, when I first arrived to the compound of the Zinc Factory, coming from the direction of Srebrenica, I was here, in this area, in the corner of this area [indicates], together with my children. And on the following day, on the second day, I moved to the Express plant, which was part of the transport company, of the bussing company, and I was here in the vicinity of the petrol station. It was a petrol station that was used by buses. That's where the spent the second night.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While we're on this particular exhibit, did you used to work in a building known as the Feros Building?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. For the past three years prior to the war, I worked there as a chief accountant. This is the factory in question, the Feros Factory. It's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're going to be referring later in your testimony to a White House that was near the Feros Building. Can you locate that particular building that we're going to be referring to in your testimony, the White House?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: The White House is situated across the street, across from the Feros Factory. I was able to see the White House from my office in the factory. My window was facing the White House, the window of my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me show you that. Would you re-examine that image again and see if your pointer is on the right building, because do you see the road that is going from the top of the image to the bottom of the image? You mentioned that the White House was across the street from the Feros Building.

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is our warehouse, and it was across the street from that [indicated]. This is the road to Bratunac and the White House is the one here [indicated].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Mrs. Omanovic. Just for clarification, you said you worked in this area for three years. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC
utterances.text: I said three years. I worked in Feros for three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is 2.29. This might be a good place to break before we go into the more substantive areas of Mrs. Omanovic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right, Mr. Harmon. I think it's much better that we adjourn now for today at this point. So we will finish with our work for today. Mrs. Omanovic, we will continue with your testimony, and we will see you again at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
